text: Location Within Hillsborough County, FL (red circle) Page14 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version The specific site envisioned for the hub within Port Tampa Bay boundaries is shown in Figure 3.2 below. The site is currently unoccupied and undeveloped, and totals approximately 16± acres in land area. The first objective of this study was to determine if the parcel was of sufficient size for a hub capable of handling at least 2 million tons of CO throughput per year. As detailed later in this report, Entr’s 2 equipment layout requires approximately 8.5 acres and therefore this objective was met. Further study revealed that the overall 16-acre parcel is of sufficient size to eventually expand to a throughput of 8 million tons per year. The proposed hub site is adjacent to deep water accessible Berth 30 which already has infrastructure installed to serve the adjacent marine terminal tenants, a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) terminal to the east, and a cement and bulk aggregate terminal to the west. PTB advises that Berth 30 is seldom used by those two adjacent tenants and would normally be readily available for Aptamus’ proposed two CO ships regularly calling on the T-RICH terminal. 2 Figure 3.2 – Proposed Hub Site Page15 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version Figure 3.3 – Proposed Hub Site and Surrounding Area As shown in Figure 3.3, the proposed hub site is completely surrounded by other industrial sites within Port Tampa Bay, and by water. The nearest retail store available to the public is 1.4 miles away. The nearest residential neighborhood is approximately 2 miles away. Because the proposed site is surrounded by other existing industrial sites of a similar nature, the site itself does not introduce an increased hazard to the immediate surrounding environment that wasn’t already there due to existing port operations. Risks unique to CO are discussed later in this report. 2 Page16 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version 3.1 GEOLOGY 3.1.1 THE STATE OF FLORIDA The land in Florida lies on the eastern side of the “Florida Platform,” a flat, sedimentary geological structure that is more than twice as wide as the state itself. It was formed millions of years ago from calcium carbonate and similar materials that were deposited from the warm, shallow ocean that fully covered it at the time. From that, limestone formed which now extends hundreds of feet below the surface. There is a karst surface above the limestone with many sinkholes, folds, sags and warps, which itself is covered by a thin layer of quartz sand which was transported over time from the Appalachian and Piedmont regions to the north. Since the end of the last ice age 20,000 years ago, global sea levels have risen approximately 122 meters covering the majority of the Florida Platform and resulting in the Florida shorelines we see today, including Tampa Bay. Furthermore, the complexity of local processes such as sedimentation and estuarian evolution (semi-enclosed coastal zones where river freshwater mixes with seawater) plays a critical role in shaping the region’s contemporary appearance.
